note: A teaching of the Sages records an incident in which Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gave a newly married virgin four nights, within the first twelve months of her marriage, during which blood after intercourse would be treated as blood of her torn hymen rather than menstrual blood. The text does not describe the case further.
why: Rav has just ruled that a grown woman is given only the first night; the Gemara raises this incident as an objection and begins asking at what age the bride was.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who grants the bride the four nights.

terms.meaning: Bleeding from first intercourse, which does not make a woman ritually impure, unlike menstrual blood.
A status that, for a menstruating woman, forbids marital relations until she purifies herself.

flag: The story is a one-line precedent and stops mid-sentence as the Gemara starts analyzing it.

note: Ravina arranged for his son to marry the daughter of Rav Hanina. Rav Hanina asked whether the marriage contract should set the wedding for Wednesday, and Ravina agreed. When Wednesday came, Ravina waited another week. Asked why, he cited Rava: a woman who accepts a marriage proposal must count seven clean days. Rav Hanina answered that Rava meant an adult woman who has seen blood, not a young girl who has not. Ravina replied that Rava had said so explicitly: the reason is that she desires her husband, and a young girl desires him too.
why: The Gemara has just cited Rava's ruling that a woman who accepts a proposal must count seven clean days; this incident shows the ruling put into practice and extends it to a girl who has not yet menstruated.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The father of the groom, who delays the wedding a week.

people.name: Rav Hanina
people.about: The father of the bride, who questions the delay.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage whose ruling Ravina follows.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, the document a groom gives his bride setting out his obligations, here also fixing the wedding date.
Seven days without any flow of blood, after which a woman immerses in a ritual bath and may resume marital relations.
